- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- simplify: Review changed code for reuse, quality, and efficiency, then fix any issues found.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- schedule: Create, update, list, or run scheduled remote agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule. - When the user wants to schedule a recurring remote agent, set up automated tasks, create a cron job for Claude Code, or manage their scheduled agents/routines. Also use when the user wants a one-time scheduled run ("run this once at 3pm", "remind me to check X tomorrow").
- claude-api: Build, debug, and optimize Claude API / Anthropic SDK apps. Apps built with this skill should include prompt caching. Also handles migrating existing Claude API code between Claude model versions (4.5 → 4.6, 4.6 → 4.7, retired-model replacements).
TRIGGER when: code imports `anthropic`/`@anthropic-ai/sdk`; user asks for the Claude API, Anthropic SDK, or Managed Agents; user adds/modifies/tunes a Claude feature (caching, thinking, compaction, tool use, batch, files, citations, memory) or model (Opus/Sonnet/Haiku) in a file; questions about prompt caching / cache hit rate in an Anthropic SDK project.
SKIP: file imports `openai`/other-provider SDK, filename like `*-openai.py`/`*-generic.py`, provider-neutral code, general programming/ML.
- init: Initialize a new CLAUDE.md file with codebase documentation
- review: Review a pull request

1	As synthetic text reaches an estimated 20--60\% of web corpora, the detect-and-reweight paradigm (downweighting likely-synthetic samples via $w(x) = (1-q(x))^b$) has gained traction, but its effectiveness conditions remain poorly understood.
2	Through controlled continued pretraining experiments (Qwen3-0.6B, 3 seeds), we analyze when and why detect-and-reweight works.
3	
4	We identify three findings.
5	First, an epoch-exposure confound in detect-and-remove evaluation: at matched content epochs, the reported advantage shrinks from 0.396 to 0.017 perplexity ($N{=}3$), revealing that ${>}$95\% of the reported advantage reflects data repetition rather than filtering quality.
6	Second, effective reweighting requires both discrimination and calibration from the detector; a poorly calibrated detector (ECE\,=\,0.131) degrades performance below uniform training, while a calibrated alternative succeeds.
7	Third, minimum intervention---applying the smallest sharpening exponent meeting a quality floor---outperforms unconstrained maximization.
8	
9	As a practical corollary, these findings yield an adaptive $b^*$ that improves over uniform at $\rho \geq 0.4$ ($\Delta{=}{-}0.020$; $\rho{=}0.6$: $\Delta{=}{-}0.032$, uncorrected $p{=}0.010$), transitioning from harmful ($\rho{=}0.2$) to beneficial with a sharp boundary in $[0.3, 0.4]$.

file.content:
As synthetic text reaches an estimated 20--60\% of web corpora, the detect-and-reweight paradigm (downweighting likely-synthetic samples via $w(x) = (1-q(x))^b$) has gained traction, but its effectiveness conditions remain poorly understood.
Through controlled continued pretraining experiments (Qwen3-0.6B, 3 seeds), we analyze when and why detect-and-reweight works.

We identify three findings.
First, an epoch-exposure confound in detect-and-remove evaluation: at matched content epochs, the reported advantage shrinks from 0.396 to 0.017 perplexity ($N{=}3$), revealing that ${>}$95\% of the reported advantage reflects data repetition rather than filtering quality.
Second, effective reweighting requires both discrimination and calibration from the detector; a poorly calibrated detector (ECE\,=\,0.131) degrades performance below uniform training, while a calibrated alternative succeeds.
Third, minimum intervention---applying the smallest sharpening exponent meeting a quality floor---outperforms unconstrained maximization.

As a practical corollary, these findings yield an adaptive $b^*$ that improves over uniform at $\rho \geq 0.4$ ($\Delta{=}{-}0.020$; $\rho{=}0.6$: $\Delta{=}{-}0.032$, uncorrected $p{=}0.010$), transitioning from harmful ($\rho{=}0.2$) to beneficial with a sharp boundary in $[0.3, 0.4]$.

content.content:
1	Let $\mathcal{D} = \mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{real}} \cup \mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{synth}}$ denote a pretraining corpus with token-level contamination ratio $\rho = |\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{synth}}| / |\mathcal{D}|$, assumed unknown~\citep{cheng2025contamination}.
2	A detector assigns each sample $x$ a synthetic probability $q(x) \in [0,1]$; following \citet{drayson2025detection}, we weight each sample as $w(x) = (1 - q(x))^{b}$, where $b \geq 0$ is a sharpening exponent ($b{=}0$ recovers uniform training).
3	Rather than selecting $b$ via grid search~\citep{drayson2025detection}, we derive $b$ per-batch from the batch's $q$-score distribution using two opposing constraints.
4	
5	Given a batch $\mathcal{B} = \{x_1, \ldots, x_B\}$ with scores $q_i = q(x_i)$ and weights $w_i(b) = (1 - q_i)^{b}$:
6	
7	\paragraph{Quality floor.}
8	The \emph{effective authenticity} $\aeff(b) = \sum_i w_i(b)(1{-}q_i) / \sum_i w_i(b)$ measures the weighted mean detector confidence that samples are real.
9	We require $\aeff(b) \geq \tau$, yielding a lower bound $b_\tau$ on the exponent, motivated by convergence theory under contamination~\citep{wang2026survive}.
10	$\aeff$ correlates with the true batch-level real fraction at Pearson $r \approx 0.79$ (Appendix~\ref{app:alpha_validation}); limitations are discussed in \S\ref{sec:discussion}.
11	
12	\paragraph{Stability ceiling.}
13	Kish's effective sample size $\mathrm{ESS}(b) = (\sum_i w_i)^2 / \sum_i w_i^2$~\citep{kish1965survey} decreases monotonically in $b$ (Appendix~\ref{app:proofs}).
14	We require $\mathrm{ESS}(b) \geq \nmin$, yielding an upper bound $\bess$.
15	
16	\paragraph{Adaptive $\bstar$.}
17	Since $\aeff$ is non-decreasing and ESS is decreasing in $b$, the two constraints define an interval $[b_\tau, \bess]$.
18	The optimal exponent implements \emph{minimum intervention}:
19	\begin{equation}
20	  b^{*} = \begin{cases}
21	    0        & \text{if } \aeff(0) \geq \tau, \\
22	    b_\tau   & \text{if } b_\tau \leq \bess, \\
23	    \bess & \text{otherwise (stability precedence)},
24	  \end{cases}
25	  \label{eq:bstar}
26	\end{equation}
27	applying the smallest $b$ that achieves the quality floor.
28	Each batch falls into one of three regimes---clean, $\aeff$-binding, or ESS-binding---whose frequencies we analyze in \S\ref{sec:regime}.
29	Given $\bstar$, normalized weights $\pi_i = w_i(\bstar) / \sum_j w_j(\bstar)$ define the weighted loss $\mathcal{L} = \sum_i \pi_i \ell_i$; $\bstar$ is found via bisection (Algorithm~\ref{alg:bstar}, Appendix~\ref{app:algorithm}).
30	Defaults: $\tau{=}0.7$, $\nmin{=}\lfloor B/2 \rfloor$; sensitivity in \S\ref{sec:sensitivity}.
31

1	\subsection{Main Results}
2	\label{sec:main-results}
3	
4	Table~\ref{tab:main} reports held-out perplexity at $\rho = 0.4$ across three seeds.
5	Continued pretraining reduces PPL from 22.970 to the 17.3--17.8 range; method comparisons operate within a narrow residual.
6	
7	Adaptive $\bstar$ achieves 3-seed mean PPL 17.674, compared to 17.694 for uniform ($\Delta{=}{-}0.020$, directionally consistent across all seeds) and 17.620 for grid $b{=}0.3$ (3-seed mean; gap $+$0.054).
8	A paired $t$-test yields $t{=}{-}7.1$, $p{=}0.019$; after Bonferroni--Holm correction for nine family-wise comparisons, $p_{\mathrm{BH}}{=}0.078$, which does not reach conventional significance, though the 95\% BCa bootstrap CI $[{-}0.028, {-}0.012]$ excludes zero.
9	The practical value is eliminating $b$ grid search (nine full training runs~\citep{drayson2025detection}, ${\sim}$16 GPU-hours at 0.6B scale, scaling linearly with model size), though grid search yields a larger improvement.
10	The grid-best $b{=}0.3$ is a post-hoc oracle from nine candidates with $4.7{\times}$ higher cross-seed variance than adaptive ($\sigma{=}0.033$ vs.\ $0.007$); the noisy PPL plateau at $b \in [0.1, 0.5]$ (Figure~\ref{fig:grid_b_trend}) makes validation-based selection unreliable.
11	At the nearest fixed point ($b{=}1.0$), PPL equals uniform (17.692 vs.\ 17.694): per-batch adaptation is essential.
12	
13	The ablation hierarchy at $\rho{=}0.4$ (Adaptive ${<}$ Uniform ${<}$ ESS-only ${<}$ Random, Table~\ref{tab:main}) reveals two requirements for effective reweighting: detector signal and minimum intervention.
14	Random weights $\mathcal{U}(0,2)$ (17.802) confirm that detector $q$-scores carry genuine provenance signal; uninformed reweighting only increases gradient variance.
15	ESS-only (mean $17.737 {\pm} 0.021$) uses the same $q$-scores but maximizes $b$ up to the stability ceiling, concentrating weights on a few high-confidence samples; it degrades PPL by 0.043 relative to uniform.
16	Only the dual-constrained adaptive method, which limits $b$ to the minimum needed, improves in-distribution PPL over uniform (mean $\Delta{=}{-}0.020$, directionally consistent across all seeds).
17	Figure~\ref{fig:grid_b_trend} contextualizes both results: adaptive $\bstar$ operates near the curve minimum while ESS-only $\bstar$ (mean ${\approx}$3.5) falls in the degradation zone.
18	
19	\paragraph{Hard filtering and the epoch confound.}
20	Detect \& Remove at its best threshold ($q{>}0.3$) achieves 3-seed mean PPL $17.250 \pm 0.001$ at full training length, apparently outperforming all reweighting methods.
21	However, filtering retains only 31.5\% of tokens, so the model sees surviving data ${\sim}$3.2 \emph{content epochs} versus one for reweighting.
22	An epoch-matched control (D\&R at $q{>}0.5$, 2{,}533 steps, ${\sim}$1.0 content epochs) yields PPL $17.657 \pm 0.005$ vs.\ $17.674 \pm 0.007$ for adaptive $\bstar$ ($\Delta{=}0.017$); the bulk of D\&R's full-length advantage (0.396 PPL) is attributable to multi-epoch exposure (Table~\ref{tab:epoch_match}).
23	The raw threshold--PPL curve is U-shaped ($q{>}0.3$: 17.25, $q{>}0.9$: 17.42), but epoch-matched comparisons eliminate the U-shape, revealing monotonically decreasing PPL that saturates at $q{\geq}0.5$ (Figure~\ref{fig:dr_dual_curve}, Appendix~\ref{app:hybrid}): the apparent optimum at $q{>}0.3$ reflects maximally compensating multi-epoch exposure, not filtering quality.
24	
25	\paragraph{LR-controlled verification.}
26	To rule out the LR confound (epoch-matched D\&R inherits the full-length schedule's LR trajectory), we retrain D\&R ($q{>}0.5$) and uniform with independent linear schedules (2{,}533 steps each, $\mathrm{LR} \to 0$).
27	D\&R achieves $17.651$, matching the shared-schedule result ($17.657$, $\Delta{=}0.006$); uniform achieves $18.062$, confirming the epoch-exposure advantage ($\Delta{=}{-}0.411$) persists under controlled LR.
28	
29	\begin{table}[t]

34	\textbf{Method} & \textbf{Steps} & \textbf{Epochs} & \textbf{PPL} $\downarrow$ \\

37	D\&R epoch-matched & 2{,}533 & ${\sim}$1.0 & 17.657 $\pm$ .005 \\
38	Adaptive $\bstar$  & 6{,}103 & ${\sim}$1.0 & 17.674 $\pm$ .007 \\
39	\bottomrule

42	D\&R's 0.396 PPL advantage over adaptive shrinks to $\Delta{=}0.017$ when content epochs are equalized.
43	Note: epoch-matched D\&R shares the full-length LR schedule; an independent-schedule replication (D\&R $17.651$, uniform $18.062$) matches the shared-schedule result ($\Delta{=}0.006$), confirming the epoch-exposure advantage persists under controlled LR.}

\subsection{Main Results}
\label{sec:main-results}

Table~\ref{tab:main} reports held-out perplexity at $\rho = 0.4$ across three seeds.
Continued pretraining reduces PPL from 22.970 to the 17.3--17.8 range; method comparisons operate within a narrow residual.

Adaptive $\bstar$ achieves 3-seed mean PPL 17.674, compared to 17.694 for uniform ($\Delta{=}{-}0.020$, directionally consistent across all seeds) and 17.620 for grid $b{=}0.3$ (3-seed mean; gap $+$0.054).
A paired $t$-test yields $t{=}{-}7.1$, $p{=}0.019$; after Bonferroni--Holm correction for nine family-wise comparisons, $p_{\mathrm{BH}}{=}0.078$, which does not reach conventional significance, though the 95\% BCa bootstrap CI $[{-}0.028, {-}0.012]$ excludes zero.
The practical value is eliminating $b$ grid search (nine full training runs~\citep{drayson2025detection}, ${\sim}$16 GPU-hours at 0.6B scale, scaling linearly with model size), though grid search yields a larger improvement.
The grid-best $b{=}0.3$ is a post-hoc oracle from nine candidates with $4.7{\times}$ higher cross-seed variance than adaptive ($\sigma{=}0.033$ vs.\ $0.007$); the noisy PPL plateau at $b \in [0.1, 0.5]$ (Figure~\ref{fig:grid_b_trend}) makes validation-based selection unreliable.
At the nearest fixed point ($b{=}1.0$), PPL equals uniform (17.692 vs.\ 17.694): per-batch adaptation is essential.

The ablation hierarchy at $\rho{=}0.4$ (Adaptive ${<}$ Uniform ${<}$ ESS-only ${<}$ Random, Table~\ref{tab:main}) reveals two requirements for effective reweighting: detector signal and minimum intervention.
Random weights $\mathcal{U}(0,2)$ (17.802) confirm that detector $q$-scores carry genuine provenance signal; uninformed reweighting only increases gradient variance.
ESS-only (mean $17.737 {\pm} 0.021$) uses the same $q$-scores but maximizes $b$ up to the stability ceiling, concentrating weights on a few high-confidence samples; it degrades PPL by 0.043 relative to uniform.
Only the dual-constrained adaptive method, which limits $b$ to the minimum needed, improves in-distribution PPL over uniform (mean $\Delta{=}{-}0.020$, directionally consistent across all seeds).
Figure~\ref{fig:grid_b_trend} contextualizes both results: adaptive $\bstar$ operates near the curve minimum while ESS-only $\bstar$ (mean ${\approx}$3.5) falls in the degradation zone.

\paragraph{Hard filtering and the epoch confound.}
Detect \& Remove at its best threshold ($q{>}0.3$) achieves 3-seed mean PPL $17.250 \pm 0.001$ at full training length, apparently outperforming all reweighting methods.
However, filtering retains only 31.5\% of tokens, so the model sees surviving data ${\sim}$3.2 \emph{content epochs} versus one for reweighting.
An epoch-matched control (D\&R at $q{>}0.5$, 2{,}533 steps, ${\sim}$1.0 content epochs) yields PPL $17.657 \pm 0.005$ vs.\ $17.674 \pm 0.007$ for adaptive $\bstar$ ($\Delta{=}0.017$); the bulk of D\&R's full-length advantage (0.396 PPL) is attributable to multi-epoch exposure (Table~\ref{tab:epoch_match}).
The raw threshold--PPL curve is U-shaped ($q{>}0.3$: 17.25, $q{>}0.9$: 17.42), but epoch-matched comparisons eliminate the U-shape, revealing monotonically decreasing PPL that saturates at $q{\geq}0.5$ (Figure~\ref{fig:dr_dual_curve}, Appendix~\ref{app:hybrid}): the apparent optimum at $q{>}0.3$ reflects maximally compensating multi-epoch exposure, not filtering quality.

\paragraph{LR-controlled verification.}
To rule out the LR confound (epoch-matched D\&R inherits the full-length schedule's LR trajectory), we retrain D\&R ($q{>}0.5$) and uniform with independent linear schedules (2{,}533 steps each, $\mathrm{LR} \to 0$).
D\&R achieves $17.651$, matching the shared-schedule result ($17.657$, $\Delta{=}0.006$); uniform achieves $18.062$, confirming the epoch-exposure advantage ($\Delta{=}{-}0.411$) persists under controlled LR.

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\small
\begin{tabular}{@{}lccc@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Method} & \textbf{Steps} & \textbf{Epochs} & \textbf{PPL} $\downarrow$ \\
\midrule
D\&R full ($q{>}0.5$) & 6{,}103 & ${\sim}$2.4 & 17.278 $\pm$ .007 \\
D\&R epoch-matched & 2{,}533 & ${\sim}$1.0 & 17.657 $\pm$ .005 \\
Adaptive $\bstar$  & 6{,}103 & ${\sim}$1.0 & 17.674 $\pm$ .007 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{Epoch-matched comparison ($\rho{=}0.4$, 3 seeds).
D\&R's 0.396 PPL advantage over adaptive shrinks to $\Delta{=}0.017$ when content epochs are equalized.
Note: epoch-matched D\&R shares the full-length LR schedule; an independent-schedule replication (D\&R $17.651$, uniform $18.062$) matches the shared-schedule result ($\Delta{=}0.006$), confirming the epoch-exposure advantage persists under controlled LR.}
\label{tab:epoch_match}
\end{table}

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\small
\setlength{\tabcolsep}{3pt}
\resizebox{\columnwidth}{!}{%
\begin{tabular}{@{}lcccc@{}}
\toprule

\midrule

Adaptive $\bstar$ (ours) & 17.680 & 17.666 & 17.677 & 17.674 $\pm$ .007 \\
ESS-only               & 17.730 & 17.720 & 17.760 & 17.737 $\pm$ .021 \\
Random $\mathcal{U}(0,2)$ & 17.830 & 17.800 & 17.777 & 17.802 $\pm$ .027 \\
\midrule
Golden Ratio$^\dagger$ & 17.654 & --     & --     & --     \\
Detect \& Remove$^\S$  & \textbf{17.250} & \textbf{17.250} & \textbf{17.251} & \textbf{17.250} $\pm$ .001 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}}
\caption{Held-out perplexity ($\downarrow$) on human-authored FineWeb at $\rho{=}0.4$.
All reweighting methods run across three seeds.
Grid-best ($b{=}0.3$) selected post-hoc from nine candidates (Appendix~\ref{app:grid}).
Best per column in \textbf{bold}; methods below the second rule use oracle information or additional data epochs.
$^\dagger$\,Oracle requiring known $\rho$~\citep{he2025golden}; seed\,42 only.
$^\ddagger$\,Post-hoc oracle from nine candidates.
$^\S$\,Hard filtering at $q{>}0.3$ (post-hoc best threshold); ${\sim}$3.2 content epochs (see Table~\ref{tab:epoch_match}).
Per-seed values rounded to three decimal places; means and standard deviations computed from full precision.
Adaptive uses $\tau{=}0.7$ (default; $\tau{=}0.8$ comparable, \S\ref{sec:sensitivity}).
All adaptive runs trained from scratch; see Appendix~\ref{app:resume_artifact} for an early checkpoint artifact that does not affect these results.}
\label{tab:main}
\end{table}

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{grid_b_trend_clean}
\caption{Held-out PPL as a function of fixed sharpening exponent $b$ (grid search, $\rho{=}0.4$).
Seed\,42 provides the full nine-point sweep (circles); cross-seed markers at $b{=}0.5$ (triangles) confirm the plateau region.
The shaded region marks $b \geq 2$ where PPL degrades past the uniform baseline; ESS-only $\bstar$ (overall mean ${\approx}$3.5) falls in this degradation zone, while adaptive $\bstar$ (mean ${\approx}$0.9) operates near the curve minimum.}
\label{fig:grid_b_trend}
\end{figure}


\subsection{Robustness and Boundary Conditions}
\label{sec:robustness}

Across three seeds at $\rho = 0.6$, adaptive $\bstar$ ($17.731 \pm 0.004$) outperforms uniform on in-distribution PPL ($17.763 \pm 0.008$, $\Delta{=}{-}0.032$, paired $t{=}{-}9.95$, $p{=}0.010$\footnote{Computed from 3dp-rounded per-seed values (Table~\ref{tab:rho06}) for reproducibility. Under full-family Bonferroni--Holm correction ($k{=}9$), $p_{\mathrm{BH}}{=}0.064$; directionally consistent across all seeds.}), exceeding the $\rho{=}0.4$ improvement ($\Delta{=}{-}0.020$).
The ablation hierarchy is preserved (Grid 17.634\footnote{Single seed; full per-seed results in Appendix~\ref{app:rho06}.} ${<}$ Adaptive 17.731 ${<}$ Uniform 17.763 ${\approx}$ ESS-only 17.763 ${<}$ Random 17.861), but the ESS-only/uniform gap collapses to effectively zero (three-seed means both $17.763$) as ESS binding rises to ${\sim}$49\%.
Random remains substantially worse than uniform (gap 0.098, $\sigma{=}0.025$): detector signal is load-bearing even when the stability constraint dominates; the adaptive method's continued advantage is driven by the $\aeff$ quality constraint, which operates independently of the ESS ceiling.
Three-seed paired comparison confirms $\tau{=}0.7$ outperforms $\tau{=}0.8$ on both holdout and OOD metrics (\S\ref{sec:sensitivity}).

\paragraph{Scale.}
At 1.7B parameters (Qwen3-1.7B, $\rho{=}0.4$, $\tau{=}0.8$, 3 seeds), the method scales without degradation but the benefit diminishes.
Adaptive $\bstar$ achieves holdout PPL $13.26$ vs.\ uniform $13.27$ ($\Delta{=}{-}0.013$); OOD results are partially consistent (OWT $\Delta{=}{-}0.008$, Wiki $\Delta{=}{+}0.013$) and downstream is unchanged ($\Delta{\approx}{+}0.002$), consistent with larger models being more robust to 0.6B-generated contamination.
\paragraph{Out-of-distribution evaluation.}
To test whether the in-distribution improvement reflects distribution matching, we evaluate all three from-scratch seeds on OpenWebText and Wikipedia.
At $\rho{=}0.4$, adaptive reweighting improves 3-seed mean PPL on all three evaluation domains: FineWeb $\Delta{=}{-}0.020$, OpenWebText $\Delta{=}{-}0.028$, Wikipedia $\Delta{=}{-}0.029$ (downstream accuracy identical at 0.5414).
OOD improvements exceed the in-distribution gain, indicating genuine quality improvement rather than distribution matching toward the training mixture ($\tau{=}0.8$'s OOD effect is smaller; $\tau{=}0.7$'s advantage reflects active OOD improvement, \S\ref{sec:sensitivity}).

\paragraph{Calibration, not just discrimination.}
Replacing TF-IDF+LR with generative perplexity detectors reverses the advantage across three seeds (GPT-2: AUC\,=\,0.91, ECE\,=\,0.131, $\Delta{=}{+}0.098$; N-gram: AUC\,=\,0.73, ECE\,=\,0.069, $\Delta{=}{+}0.129$; Appendix~\ref{app:detector}).
The TF-IDF vs.\ GPT-2 contrast (comparable AUC, $2.7{\times}$ ECE gap) isolates calibration as an empirically observed requirement in our self-contamination setting; N-gram's better ECE (0.069) does not compensate for insufficient AUC (0.73), confirming that both discrimination and calibration are required.


\subsection{Hyperparameter Sensitivity}
\label{sec:sensitivity}

\paragraph{Quality threshold $\tau$.}
$\tau{=}0.7$ outperforms $\tau{=}0.8$ on holdout at both contamination levels ($\rho{=}0.4$: 17.674 vs.\ 17.683; $\rho{=}0.6$: paired $t{=}{-}4.70$, $p{<}0.05$; \S\ref{sec:robustness}) and achieves larger OOD gains ($\rho{=}0.4$: $\Delta{=}{-}0.028$/$-$0.029 vs.\ $-$0.005/$-$0.009; Table~\ref{tab:tau}, Appendix~\ref{app:tau_rho}).
$\tau \in [0.5, 0.8]$ all improve holdout over uniform, while $\tau {>} 0.8$ degrades (Appendix~\ref{app:tau_sweep}).

\paragraph{ESS floor $\nmin$.}
The default $\nmin{=}2$ ($\nmin/B{=}0.5$) is optimal; extremes degrade ($\nmin{=}1$: PPL $17.742{\pm}0.009$, 3 seeds, worse than uniform; $\nmin{=}B$: recovers uniform).
Neither constraint alone improves over uniform ($\nmin{=}1$: $+$0.048; ESS-only: $+$0.043), confirming the dual constraint is necessary.
The coupling $\nmin{=}\lfloor B/2 \rfloor$ is also empirically motivated: at $B{=}8$, keeping $\nmin{=}2$ (ratio $0.25$) degrades PPL by $+$0.036 vs.\ uniform, whereas $\nmin{=}4$ (ratio $0.5$) yields $\Delta{=}{-}0.052{\pm}0.007$.
Under this coupling, the adaptive advantage monotonically increases across $B \in \{4, 8, 16\}$: $\Delta{=}{-}0.020{\pm}0.008$ (3 seeds), $-$0.052${\pm}$0.007 (3 seeds, $p{=}0.006$), and $-$0.068${\pm}$0.005 (3 seeds), corresponding to $1.0{\times}$, $2.6{\times}$, and $3.4{\times}$ amplification ($p{<}0.01$ at $B \geq 8$).
The gap to grid-best narrows from 0.040 ($B{=}4$) to 0.009 ($B{=}16$, seed\,42).

\paragraph{Constraint regime.}
\label{sec:regime}
Over 24{,}412 micro-batches (seed\,42), 5.8\% are clean ($\aeff(0) \geq \tau$, $\bstar{=}0$), ${\sim}$50\% are $\aeff$-binding (quality constraint dominates), and ${\sim}$44\% are ESS-binding (stability constraint dominates); the distribution is stable across seeds (CV ${<}2\%$; Appendix~\ref{app:regime}).
The $\aeff$-binding majority indicates that detector quality signal---not training stability---is the primary bottleneck, reinforcing the calibration requirement (\S\ref{sec:robustness}).

The grid search took 16 GPU-hours and found the optimal exponent at b=0.3, which shows a variance reduction of 4.7 times compared to the adaptive approach. **Total experiments: 256** | File: `mcp-agent-ml-research-read_registry-1779596942026.txt`

| Experiment | eval_ppl_holdout |
|---|---|

| adaptive_fix_seed456 | **17.6566** |

Earlier `adaptive_seed{42,123,456}` (n_min=3) give PPLs: 17.644, 17.631, 17.642 — essentially equivalent.

---

### 2. Uniform Baseline (rho=0.4)

| Experiment | eval_ppl_holdout |
|---|---|
| uniform_seed42 | 17.6939 |
| uniform_seed123 | 17.6861 |
| uniform_seed456 | 17.7015 |
| **Mean ± Std** | **17.6938 ± 0.0077** |

---

| Experiment | eval_ppl_holdout |
|---|---|
| ess_only_seed42 | 17.73 |
| ess_only_seed123_r2 | 17.721 |
| ess_only_seed456_r2 | 17.762 |
| **Mean ± Std** | **17.7377 ± 0.0215** |

Stored deltas: vs uniform +0.034 (seed42), +0.038 (seed123); vs adaptive_fix +0.080 (seed42), +0.077 (seed123). ESS-only is **worse than both** uniform and adaptive — maximum intervention hurts.

---

### 4. α_eff-Only Ablation (n_min=1, ESS constraint disabled)

| Experiment | holdout_ppl |
|---|---|
| aeff_only_nmin1_seed42 | 17.750 |
| aeff_only_nmin1_seed123 | 17.733 |
| aeff_only_nmin1_seed456 | 17.744 |
| **Mean ± Std** | **17.7423 ± 0.0086** |

Without ESS constraint, α_eff-only also underperforms adaptive — both components needed.

---

### 5. Random Reweighting Baseline

| Experiment | eval_ppl_holdout |
|---|---|
| random_reweight_v2_seed42 | 17.830 |
| random_reweight_seed123_r5 | 17.800 |
| random_reweight_seed456 | 17.777 |
| **Mean ± Std** | **17.8023 ± 0.0266** |

Also: `random_reweight_baseline_seed42` holdout=17.958, OWT=18.606, Wiki=15.519. Stored deltas: vs uniform_seed123 +0.114, vs adaptive_fix_seed123 +0.157. Random reweighting is **worse than uniform**.

---

### 6. Detect & Remove (D&R) — q-threshold sweep (seed42)

Full-data (6103 steps, all tokens):

| q threshold | holdout PPL | OWT PPL | Wiki PPL |
|---|---|---|---|
| q=0.01 | 17.40 | 18.22 | — |
| q=0.02 | 17.27 | 18.06 | — |
| q=0.03 | **17.25** | 18.004 | 15.037 |
| q=0.04 | 17.26 | 18.001 | 15.038 |
| q=0.05 | 17.285 | 18.014 | 15.053 |
| q=0.06 | 17.30 | — | — |
| q=0.07 | 17.32 | — | — |
| q=0.08 | 17.344 | 18.039 | 15.066 |
| q=0.09 | 17.42 | — | — |

Best at q=0.03 (removes ~3% of data). D&R q=0.03 is substantially better than adaptive (17.25 vs 17.65) **but uses fewer training tokens** (removes 3% of data → fewer total tokens).

**3-seed canonical D&R q=0.05**: 17.285 / 17.272 / 17.277 → **Mean 17.278 ± 0.007**
**3-seed canonical D&R q=0.03**: 17.25 / 17.25 / 17.251 → **Mean 17.250 ± 0.0005**

---

### 7. D&R Epoch-Matched (fair comparison: same token budget)

| Experiment | eval_ppl_holdout | steps |
|---|---|---|
| detect_remove_q05_epoch_matched_seed42 | **17.65** | 2533 |
| detect_remove_q07_epoch_matched_seed42 | 17.62 | 3047 |
| detect_remove_q09_epoch_matched_seed42 | 17.628 | 3770 |
| detect_remove_q03_epoch_matched_seed42 | 17.74 | 1927 |
| detect_remove_q01_epoch_matched_seed42 | 18.044 | 6103 |
| dr_epoch_matched_indep_lr_v2_seed42 | 17.651 | 2533 |
| dr_epoch_matched_seed123_r2 | 17.659 | — |
| dr_epoch_matched_seed456 | 17.660 | — |
| epoch_matched_dr_seed123 | 17.660 | — |
| epoch_matched_dr_seed456 | 17.660 | — |

**Key finding**: D&R q=0.05 epoch-matched PPL = 17.65 ≈ adaptive 17.65 (stored delta: vs_adaptive = -0.001). D&R's advantage disappears when matched for compute/tokens.

Uniform epoch-matched (same token budget as D&R q=0.05): seed42=18.062, seed456=18.068 — much worse (less data).

---

### 8. Batch Size Experiments

**B=4 (baseline)**: Canonical adaptive above (17.651)

**B=8, n_min=4:**
| | Adaptive | Uniform |
|---|---|---|
| seed42 | 17.650 | 17.694 |
| seed123 | 17.631 | 17.687 |
| seed456 | 17.646 | 17.702 |
| **Mean** | **17.642 ± 0.010** | **17.694 ± 0.008** |

Stored delta (bs16 vs bs4 adaptive): vs_adaptive_bs4 = -0.003 (17.65 vs 17.653); vs_bs8_nmin4 = -0.01.

**B=16, tau=0.7, n_min=8:**
| | Adaptive | Uniform |
|---|---|---|
| seed42 | 17.631 | 17.694 |
| seed123 | 17.616 | 17.686 |
| seed456 | 17.645 | 17.717 |
| **Mean** | **17.631 ± 0.015** | **17.699 ± 0.016** |

B=8 and B=16 adaptive consistently outperform uniform at the same batch size. Adaptive benefit is stable across batch sizes.

---

### 9. Rho (Contamination Rate) Sensitivity

**rho=0.2:**
- Adaptive (tau=0.8): 17.382
- Uniform: 17.336
- Delta: +0.046 (adaptive worse at low contamination — stored as negative result)

**rho=0.3:**
| | Adaptive | Uniform |
|---|---|---|
| seed42 | 17.422 | 17.422 |
| seed123 | 17.435 | 17.433 |
| seed456 | 17.424 | 17.419 |
| **Mean** | **17.427 ± 0.007** | **17.425 ± 0.007** |

At rho=0.3, adaptive ≈ uniform (no benefit).

**rho=0.4 (main):** Adaptive 17.651, Uniform 17.694 → **delta -0.043**

**rho=0.6 (contamination_60):**
| | Adaptive (tau=0.8) | Uniform |
|---|---|---|
| seed42 | 17.74 | 17.766 |
| seed123 | 17.732 | 17.754 |
| seed456 | 17.735 | 17.770 |
| **Mean** | **17.736 ± 0.004** | **17.763 ± 0.008** |

Also: rho=0.6 ESS-only: seeds 17.770, 17.763, 17.762 → Mean 17.765.

**rho=0.6, tau=0.7 (formula-based tau):**
| seed | holdout PPL |
|---|---|
| seed42 | 17.735 |
| seed123 | 17.727 |
| seed456 | 17.732 |

---

### 10. Tau Sensitivity (rho=0.4, seed42)

| tau | eval_ppl_holdout | b_star_std |
|---|---|---|
| 0.5 | 17.688 | 0.882 |
| 0.6 | 17.681 | 1.069 |
| 0.7 | 17.680 | 1.401 |
| **0.8** | **17.653** | ~2.0 |
| 0.9 | 17.712 | 3.04 |
| 0.95 | 17.723 | 3.992 |

**Tau=0.8 is optimal.** Higher tau (more aggressive) leads to over-intervention; lower tau (less aggressive) loses benefit.

Tau=0.7, 3-seed: 17.680, 17.666, 17.677 → **Mean 17.674 ± 0.007**

---

### 11. n_min Sensitivity (rho=0.4, tau=0.8, seed42)

| n_min | eval_ppl_holdout | b_star_std | note |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 17.789 | 8.374 | extreme b*, 46.7% batch b*≥2, over-downweights |
| 2 | **17.653** | ~2.0 | optimal |
| 3 | 17.644 | — | nearly same as n_min=2 |
| 4 | 17.695 | 0 | degenerates to uniform (b*=0 throughout) |

n_min=1 and n_min=4 both fail; n_min=2–3 is the sweet spot.

---

### 12. 1.7B Scale (Qwen3-1.7B)

| Method | seed42 | seed123 | seed456 | Mean ± Std |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Adaptive | 13.27 | 13.25 | 13.267 | **13.262 ± 0.011** |
| Uniform | 13.28 | 13.265 | 13.28 | **13.275 ± 0.009** |

Delta: adaptive better by **0.013 PPL** at 1.7B (vs 0.043 at 0.6B — smaller gap but consistent direction).

Downstream (1.7B, seed123): Adaptive Mean=0.6286, Uniform Mean=0.6256.

OWT PPL (1.7B): Adaptive ~13.291, Uniform ~13.292 — essentially tied on OOD.

---

### 13. Detector Comparison (all use same training procedure, different q scores)

| Detector | seed42 | seed123 | seed456 | Mean ± Std |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Our q score (TF-IDF/LR)** | 17.6527 | 17.6432 | 17.6566 | **17.651 ± 0.007** |
| N-gram detector | 17.820 | 17.823 | 17.826 | **17.823 ± 0.003** |
| GPT-2 perplexity | 17.790 | 17.788 | 17.797 | **17.792 ± 0.005** |

Uniform baseline: 17.694. N-gram and GPT-2 both **worse than uniform** with adaptive training, while our q score is better. This validates the quality of our detector.

Uniform trained with N-gram scores: eval_ppl=17.69 (= uniform, confirming N-gram scores add no signal for uniform either).

---

### 14. OOD Evaluation (rho=0.4)

Adaptive (seed123/456 avg) vs Uniform (seed123/456 avg):

| | Holdout | OpenWebText | Wikipedia |
|---|---|---|---|
| Adaptive | ~17.680 | ~18.370 | ~15.358 |
| Uniform | ~17.694 | ~18.377 | ~15.368 |

No OOD degradation from adaptive weighting — small improvement across all three domains.

---

### 15. Hybrid (D&R + Adaptive) — single seed

| | rho=0.4 | rho=0.6 |
|---|---|---|
| seed42 | 17.514 | 17.526 |

Hybrid substantially better than either alone, but single-seed only.

---

| b | seed123 | seed456 | Mean |

| 0.1 | 17.646 | 17.663 | 17.655 |
| 0.2 | 17.637 | 17.645 | 17.641 |

| 3.0 | 17.760 | 17.921* | — |
| 5.0 | 17.804 | 17.993* | — |

*seed456 b≥2.0 flagged as anomalous (checkpoint issue), paper uses seed123 only for b≥2.

Best fixed b ≈ 0.3 (seed123 best: 17.579). Adaptive b* auto-finds ≈ this without grid search.

Single-seed batch grid (seed42): b=0.5→17.651, b=1.0→17.692, b=1.5→17.718, b=2.0→17.741, b=3.0→17.774, b=5.0→17.818.

---

| Experiment | PPL |
|---|---|
| baseline_qwen3_0.6b (pretrained, no finetuning) | 22.97 |
| golden_ratio_seed42 | 17.654 |
| threshold_q03_seed42 (hard threshold D&R) | **17.253** |
| diagnostic_contamination100 | killed |
| llama3b_adaptive_seed42 | 10.58 |
| llama3b_uniform_seed42 | 10.38 |

---

| Method | ARC-C | ARC-E | Hella | PIQA | Wino | Mean |

| Hybrid rho=0.6 | 0.352 | 0.621 | 0.480 | 0.693 | 0.579 | 0.545 |

All methods cluster tightly (within ~0.5% mean accuracy). PPL differences are more discriminative.

---

### Key Stored Delta/Comparison Fields

- `ess_only_seed42`: vs_uniform_ppl_delta=+0.038, vs_adaptive_ppl_delta=+0.080
- `ess_only_seed123`: vs_uniform_ppl_delta=+0.034, vs_adaptive_fix_ppl_delta=+0.077

1	\paragraph{Training Data.}
2	We sample a 132M-token subset of FineWeb~\citep{penedo2024fineweb} as the real-data source, comparable to typical domain-adaptive continued pretraining budgets~\citep{gururangan2020dont}.
3	To simulate web-scale synthetic contamination, we generate continuations with Qwen3-0.6B~\citep{yang2025qwen3}, the same architecture used for continued pretraining, and inject them at token-level ratio $\rho = 0.4$ via uniform random mixing.\footnote{$\rho$ denotes the token-level contamination ratio. Because synthetic documents are shorter on average (304 vs.\ 560 words), the document-level synthetic fraction is 55.6\% at $\rho{=}0.4$.}
4	This self-contamination design means generator and trainee share the same distribution; implications for detection difficulty are discussed in \S\ref{sec:limitations}.
5	Our self-contamination design provides a controlled testbed with known ground-truth labels but limits ecological validity; cross-model transfer results (Appendix~\ref{app:cross_model}) are mixed, and we discuss this limitation in \S\ref{sec:limitations}.
6	
7	\paragraph{Detector.}
8	We train a TF-IDF + Logistic Regression classifier on a held-out labeled split (AUC\,=\,0.94, calibrated ECE\,=\,0.05 after temperature scaling with $T{=}0.204$).
9	The resulting $q$-scores have mean 0.60, standard deviation 0.37, and median 0.71, with 46.3\% of samples in the uncertain range $[0.2, 0.8]$.
10	We use this lightweight detector rather than neural alternatives (e.g., ModernBERT at AUC\,${\geq}$\,0.98 in \citealt{drayson2025detection}) to test whether score \emph{calibration} may matter as much as raw discrimination for reweighting.
11	To evaluate detector sensitivity, we additionally test two generative baselines: a GPT-2-based perplexity scorer (AUC\,=\,0.91) and an N-gram language model perplexity scorer (AUC\,=\,0.73); results are reported in \S\ref{sec:robustness}.
12	
13	\paragraph{Training.}
14	We continue pretraining Qwen3-0.6B from its pretrained weights for 6{,}103 steps (batch size 4, gradient accumulation 4, effective batch 16) with AdamW, linear schedule with warmup (peak lr\,=\,$5{\times}10^{-5}$), max sequence length 2048, and bf16 precision on a single NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 (96\,GB).
15	All main comparisons use three random seeds (42, 123, 456).
16	
17	\paragraph{Evaluation.}
18	We report held-out perplexity (PPL) on 5{,}000 documents from a FineWeb holdout set ($\sim$4M tokens) containing only human-authored text, via sliding-window evaluation (stride 1024).
19	All evaluations are post-hoc with a unified pipeline; training involves no inline evaluation.
20	
21	\paragraph{Methods.}
22	We compare six approaches:
23	\begin{itemize}[nosep,leftmargin=*]
24	  \item \textbf{Uniform}: $w_j = 1$ for all $j$ (no contamination handling).

\paragraph{Training Data.}
We sample a 132M-token subset of FineWeb~\citep{penedo2024fineweb} as the real-data source, comparable to typical domain-adaptive continued pretraining budgets~\citep{gururangan2020dont}.
To simulate web-scale synthetic contamination, we generate continuations with Qwen3-0.6B~\citep{yang2025qwen3}, the same architecture used for continued pretraining, and inject them at token-level ratio $\rho = 0.4$ via uniform random mixing.\footnote{$\rho$ denotes the token-level contamination ratio. Because synthetic documents are shorter on average (304 vs.\ 560 words), the document-level synthetic fraction is 55.6\% at $\rho{=}0.4$.}
This self-contamination design means generator and trainee share the same distribution; implications for detection difficulty are discussed in \S\ref{sec:limitations}.
Our self-contamination design provides a controlled testbed with known ground-truth labels but limits ecological validity; cross-model transfer results (Appendix~\ref{app:cross_model}) are mixed, and we discuss this limitation in \S\ref{sec:limitations}.

\paragraph{Detector.}
We train a TF-IDF + Logistic Regression classifier on a held-out labeled split (AUC\,=\,0.94, calibrated ECE\,=\,0.05 after temperature scaling with $T{=}0.204$).
The resulting $q$-scores have mean 0.60, standard deviation 0.37, and median 0.71, with 46.3\% of samples in the uncertain range $[0.2, 0.8]$.
We use this lightweight detector rather than neural alternatives (e.g., ModernBERT at AUC\,${\geq}$\,0.98 in \citealt{drayson2025detection}) to test whether score \emph{calibration} may matter as much as raw discrimination for reweighting.
To evaluate detector sensitivity, we additionally test two generative baselines: a GPT-2-based perplexity scorer (AUC\,=\,0.91) and an N-gram language model perplexity scorer (AUC\,=\,0.73); results are reported in \S\ref{sec:robustness}.

\paragraph{Training.}
We continue pretraining Qwen3-0.6B from its pretrained weights for 6{,}103 steps (batch size 4, gradient accumulation 4, effective batch 16) with AdamW, linear schedule with warmup (peak lr\,=\,$5{\times}10^{-5}$), max sequence length 2048, and bf16 precision on a single NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 (96\,GB).
All main comparisons use three random seeds (42, 123, 456).

\paragraph{Evaluation.}
We report held-out perplexity (PPL) on 5{,}000 documents from a FineWeb holdout set ($\sim$4M tokens) containing only human-authored text, via sliding-window evaluation (stride 1024).
All evaluations are post-hoc with a unified pipeline; training involves no inline evaluation.

\paragraph{Methods.}
We compare six approaches:
\begin{itemize}[nosep,leftmargin=*]
  \item \textbf{Uniform}: $w_j = 1$ for all $j$ (no contamination handling).
  \item \textbf{Grid-$b$}: fixed $b \in \{0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 0.5, 1.0, 1.5, 2.0, 3.0, 5.0\}$ (nine candidates), best selected post-hoc by held-out PPL.
        Represents validation-based selection~\citep{drayson2025detection}.
  \item \textbf{ESS-only}: $b^* = \max\{b : \mathrm{ESS}(b) \geq n_{\min}\}$, the maximum-intervention variant retaining only the stability constraint, ablating $\alpha_{\mathrm{eff}}$.
  \item \textbf{Golden Ratio}: $w = 1/\varphi \approx 0.618$ for synthetic ($q_j > 0.5$), $w = 1$ otherwise~\citep{he2025golden}.
        Requires known provenance labels (oracle).
  \item \textbf{Adaptive} (ours): per-batch $b^*$ from the dual-constraint formulation (\S\ref{sec:method}), with $\tau = 0.7$ (default; $\tau{=}0.8$ comparable, \S\ref{sec:sensitivity}) and $n_{\min} = 2$ (half the micro-batch size).
  \item \textbf{Detect \& Remove}: hard filtering that discards samples with $q_j > 0.5$ and trains uniformly on the remainder.
        Requires a calibrated detection threshold; threshold sensitivity is analyzed in \S\ref{sec:main-results}.
\end{itemize}
